newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - French markets slump on vote, stocks hit most.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - French markets slump on vote, stocks hit most.

text.p: The French franc, stocks and bonds fell sharply on Monday after the left unexpectedly won the first round of a parliamentary election.
The stockmarket took the hardest hit, opening down nearly four percent as investors who had bet on a conservative victory took cover ahead of the runoff election on June 1.
"The stock market, putting its trust in opinion polls showing the right would win, had treated the election as a non-event. We are going to pay for it," a dealer said.
The blue-chip CAC-40 index opened down 3.84 percent at 2,656.87 but steadied within the first half hour and was trading 2.9 percent lower at 2,682.31 at 0940 GMT.
The franc and bond prices also stabilised above their lows, but traders and analysts cautioned that the French markets would be nervous until the final vote next Sunday.

With most votes counted, the Interior Ministry said on Monday that the combined left had polled 40.23 percent, the ruling RPR-UDF coalition and other right-wing candidates 36.51 percent and the far-right National Front 14.90 percent. Ecologists scored 6.81 percent.
"There's nervousness because no one knows where we are. The polls were roughly right in terms of the share of the votes, but were totally wrong on the sharing of seats," a trader said.
The franc, which fell to 3.3755 to the German mark after the first projections on Sunday night putting the left ahead, sank further to 3.3773 before steading at 3.3750 at mid-morning.
A trader at a French bank said he did not expect the franc to fall much below 3.3825 on the view that a European single currency was unlikely to be derailed by a Socialist government.
"The only risk is that the foreigners will be wary of the Communists," he said.
June PIBOR futures opened 17 basis points lower at 96.30 and slumped as much as 34 basis points before climbing back to 96.30.
The June bond futures contract, which dropped as low as 128, was trading at 128.48 at mid-morning.

Traders said after the initial knee-jerk negative reaction cash-rich French domestic investors were stepping in to buy bonds along the curve at the higher yields, bringing the 10-year spread with Bunds back to minus 10, after touching minus three.

"There's plenty of cash out there and they're going to have to buy come what may, there's a tendency to buy on dips. The political debate is almost a sideshow for many of these people," a trader at a French bank said.
Markets initially shuddered at the prospect of a "co-habitation" between conservative President Jacques Chirac and a government led by the Socialists and their Communist allies.
The shock was biggest in the share market where the risk had not been priced in.

Morgan Stanley economist Eric Chaney told Reuters Financial Television he expected a two-stage fall in the bourse, the initial disappointment on Monday and then further selling on Tuesday when foreign investors returned to the market.
The U.S. and British markets are closed on Monday for holidays.
Among the biggest losers, shares in defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF were down 5.49 percent on concern that a Socialist-led government would try to block the privatisation.
Carmaker Renault's stock was down 4.03 percent on concerns its restructuring plans, entailing job losses, might also be held up by a government on the left.
